introduction: “Every undertaking is dependent upon three things: knowledge, decision, executive power.” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá often made the point that knowing what is good, and even resolving on it, accomplishes nothing without a power to carry it out; in the individual that power is faith or love, and in the world it is an institution able to enforce what the nations have agreed. The guide moves from the first sense to the second, ending with Shoghi Effendi’s world executive. Paul’s “to will is present with me; but how to perform … I find not”, James’s “faith without works is dead” and the parable of the two sons are the scriptural statements of the gap; Hamlet is its portrait. Wilson and Tennyson share the institutional hope; Montesquieu and Kant state the classic cautions about executive power.
questions: Where, in your experience, does a good intention usually fail: at knowledge, at decision, or at execution?
Reading 5 calls faith the executive power. What does faith supply that knowledge and resolve lack?
Kant feared that a world government would become a despotism. What safeguards do readings 15 to 17 mention?
Is the League of Nations’ failure evidence for ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s point?

outside.why: Knowledge, decision, executive power. Paul had the first two: to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not.
An officer planning campaigns with pins on paper. Hamlet: enterprises of great pith and moment with this regard their currents turn awry, and lose the name of action.
Without knowledge, volition and action nothing is executed. As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.
A programme of laws needs an executive force. One son said, I go, sir: and went not.
The power of faith is the executive power; the teachings are the legislative. Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, but he that doeth the will of my Father.

Montesquieu wanted the two powers kept in different hands: when the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, there can be no liberty. The reading uses the pair as a figure for teachings and faith. Does his warning have any bearing on the institutions described in readings 8 and 15 to 17?
Laxity in deeds among those certain of the truth. Be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Clerics who shouted for war fled at the first blow. What king, going to make war, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able?
Administrators who weighed the spiritual consequences of their decisions. Aristotle: most people do not do these, but take refuge in theory and think they are being philosophers.

The benefits of peace are recognized, but knowledge is not enough; a power to carry it out is needed. Wilson’s fourteenth point: a general association of nations must be formed under specific covenants.
The Supreme Tribunal which the League was not. Tennyson’s hope: the Parliament of man, the Federation of the world.

A world super-state to which nations cede the right to make war. Kant preferred a federation of separate states to their fusion under one power, because laws lose force as government widens, and a soulless despotism ends in anarchy. How do readings 15 to 17 answer that fear?

A world commonwealth with an executive and a tribunal. George Eliot ends Middlemarch elsewhere: the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts. How much of the reading’s vision depends on institutions, and how much on what she describes?

shortfall: Readings 8, 10, 11, 13 and 16 are stories or administrative clarifications to which nothing was fitted.
